claim: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is caused by mutations in the Survival Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene.
source: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is caused by mutations in the Survival Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Lefebvre et al., 1995; Lefebvre et al., 1997; Crawford and Pardo, 1996) in the Introduction section.

claim: Fatty liver has been observed in SMA mouse models and SMA patients.
source: Notably, fatty liver has been observed in SMA mouse models and SMA patients.
evidence: This statement is presented as an established observation in the field, supported by the broader context of the manuscript and prior research.

claim: Liver-specific SMN depletion does not induce motor neuron death at P19.
source: The liver-specific SMN depletion does not induce motor neuron death, neuromuscular pathology or muscle atrophy, characteristics typically observed in the Smn2B/- mouse at P19.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in motor neuron counts in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice compared to controls (Figure 4).

claim: Liver-specific SMN depletion does not induce neuromuscular pathology at P19.
source: The liver-specific SMN depletion does not induce motor neuron death, neuromuscular pathology or muscle atrophy, characteristics typically observed in the Smn2B/- mouse at P19.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in NMJ pathology in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice compared to controls (Figure 5).

claim: Liver-specific SMN depletion does not induce muscle atrophy at P19.
source: The liver-specific SMN depletion does not induce motor neuron death, neuromuscular pathology or muscle atrophy, characteristics typically observed in the Smn2B/- mouse at P19.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in muscle fiber size in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice compared to controls (Figure 6).

claim: Mild liver steatosis was observed in liver-specific SMN-depleted mice at P19.
source: However, mild liver steatosis was observed, although no changes in liver function were detected.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis (H&E and Oil Red-O staining) and triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: No changes in liver function were detected in liver-specific SMN-depleted mice at P19.
source: However, mild liver steatosis was observed, although no changes in liver function were detected.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of liver function markers (HO, transferrin, P62, IGF-1) shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Liver-specific SMN-depleted mice show a decrease in insulin-producing β-cells at P19.
source: Notably, pancreatic alterations resembled that of Smn2B/-mice, with a decrease in insulin-producing β-cells and an increase in glucagon-producingα-cells, accompanied by a reduction in blood glucose and an increase in plasma glucagon and glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing reduced insulin-positive cells in pancreatic islets (Figure 3A, B).

claim: Liver-specific SMN-depleted mice show an increase in glucagon-producing α-cells at P19.
source: Notably, pancreatic alterations resembled that of Smn2B/-mice, with a decrease in insulin-producing β-cells and an increase in glucagon-producingα-cells, accompanied by a reduction in blood glucose and an increase in plasma glucagon and glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing increased glucagon-positive cells in pancreatic islets (Figure 3A, F).

claim: Liver-specific SMN-depleted mice show a reduction in blood glucose at P19.
source: Notably, pancreatic alterations resembled that of Smn2B/-mice, with a decrease in insulin-producing β-cells and an increase in glucagon-producingα-cells, accompanied by a reduction in blood glucose and an increase in plasma glucagon and glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1).
evidence: This is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Liver-specific SMN-depleted mice show an increase in plasma glucagon at P19.
source: Notably, pancreatic alterations resembled that of Smn2B/-mice, with a decrease in insulin-producing β-cells and an increase in glucagon-producingα-cells, accompanied by a reduction in blood glucose and an increase in plasma glucagon and glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1).
evidence: This is supported by plasma glucagon measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Liver-specific SMN-depleted mice show an increase in plasma GLP-1 at P19.
source: Notably, pancreatic alterations resembled that of Smn2B/-mice, with a decrease in insulin-producing β-cells and an increase in glucagon-producingα-cells, accompanied by a reduction in blood glucose and an increase in plasma glucagon and glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1).
evidence: This is supported by plasma GLP-1 measurements shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The pancreatic and liver changes in liver-specific SMN-depleted mice were transient, with recovery observed at P60.
source: These changes were transient, as mice at P60 exhibited recovery of liver and pancreatic function.
evidence: This is supported by histological and functional data at P60 showing normalization of liver and pancreatic parameters (Figure 7).

claim: The mosaic pattern of Cre-mediated excision precludes definitive conclusions regarding the contribution of liver-specific SMN depletion to overall tissue pathology.
source: While the mosaic pattern of the Cre-mediated excision precludes definitive conclusions regarding the contribution of liver-specific SMN depletion to overall tissue pathology, our findings highlight an intricate connection between liver function and pancreatic abnormalities in SMA.
evidence: This is based on the observation of variable Cre expression across hepatocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and the interpretation of the experimental limitations.

claim: There is an intricate connection between liver function and pancreatic abnormalities in SMA.
source: While the mosaic pattern of the Cre-mediated excision precludes definitive conclusions regarding the contribution of liver-specific SMN depletion to overall tissue pathology, our findings highlight an intricate connection between liver function and pancreatic abnormalities in SMA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that liver-specific SMN depletion leads to pancreatic dysfunction without affecting pancreatic SMN levels.

claim: SMA is a hereditary neuromuscular disorder widely acknowledged as one of the leading genetic causes of infant mortality.
source: Insufficient levels of Survival Motor Neuron (SMN) protein, primarily arising from mutations or deletions in the SMN1 gene, are the root cause of spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), a hereditary neuromuscular disorder widely acknowledged as one of the leading genetic causes of infant mortality (Lefebvre et al., 1995; Lefebvre et al., 1997; Crawford and Pardo, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: SMA is characterized by the loss of motor neurons.
source: Characterized by the loss of motor neurons, SMA presents as a progressive weakening of muscle strength, primarily impacting proximal muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMA pathology, supported by the citation (Finkel et al., 2016).

claim: SMA presents as a progressive weakening of muscle strength, primarily impacting proximal muscles.
source: Characterized by the loss of motor neurons, SMA presents as a progressive weakening of muscle strength, primarily impacting proximal muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMA clinical presentation, supported by the citation (Finkel et al., 2016).

claim: If left untreated, SMA deterioration culminates in respiratory failure and premature mortality.
source: If left untreated, this deterioration culminates in respiratory failure and premature mortality (Finkel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Humans harbor two copies of the SMN gene, SMN1 and SMN2.
source: Humans harbor two copies of the SMN gene, SMN1 and SMN2, which share a nearly identical sequence except for a critical C to T substitution at position 6 of exon 7 in SMN2 (Lorson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established genetic knowledge about the SMN genes, supported by citation.

claim: SMN1 and SMN2 share a nearly identical sequence except for a critical C to T substitution at position 6 of exon 7 in SMN2.
source: Humans harbor two copies of the SMN gene, SMN1 and SMN2, which share a nearly identical sequence except for a critical C to T substitution at position 6 of exon 7 in SMN2 (Lorson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The C to T substitution in SMN2 disrupts splicing of the gene, resulting in the predominant production of an unstable protein lacking exon 7, known as SMNΔ7.
source: This single nucleotide change disrupts splicing of the gene, resulting in the predominant production of an unstable protein lacking exon 7, known as SMNΔ7 (Lorson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Approximately 10% of functional full-length (FL) SMN protein is still produced by the SMN2 gene.
source: Despite this, approximately 10% of functional full-length (FL) SMN protein is still produced by the SMN2 gene (Lefebvre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The SMN2 gene serves as a modifier of disease phenotype, with a higher copy number correlating with milder disease severity.
source: Consequently, the SMN2 gene serves as a modifier of disease phenotype, with a higher copy number correlating with milder disease severity (Feldkötter et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Mice possess a single copy of the Smn1 gene.
source: In contrast, mice possess a single copy of the Smn1 gene (Lefebvre et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Homozygous deletion of the Smn1 gene in mice induces morphological alterations and degenerative changes in embryos post-morula stage, ultimately resulting in death at preimplantation stage.
source: Notably, while homozygous deletion of both SMN genes has not been observed in humans, the homozygous deletion of the Smn1 gene in mice induces morphological alterations and degenerative changes in embryos post-morula stage, ultimately resulting in death at preimplantation stage (Schrank et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The SMN gene plays a pivotal role in early embryonic development.
source: This underscores the pivotal role of the SMN gene in early embryonic development (Vitte et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the lethality of Smn1 deletion in mice and supported by citation.

claim: SMN depletion impacts tissues beyond motor neurons, including the liver and pancreas in both SMA patients and mouse models of SMA.
source: Recent research has unveiled the extensive impact of SMN depletion beyond motor neurons, implicating additional tissues such as the liver and pancreas in both SMA patients and mouse models of SMA (Bowerman et al., 2014; Bowerman et al., 2012a; Bowerman et al., 2012b; Deguise et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Major therapeutic advancements focusing on restoring SMN levels have notably enhanced both lifespan and quality of life in SMA patients.
source: Despite major therapeutic advancements focusing on restoring SMN levels, which have notably enhanced both lifespan and quality of life in SMA patients, complete phenotypic rescue remains elusive (Finkel et al., 2016; Chiriboga, 2017; McMillan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Complete phenotypic rescue in SMA patients remains elusive despite therapeutic advancements.
source: Despite major therapeutic advancements focusing on restoring SMN levels, which have notably enhanced both lifespan and quality of life in SMA patients, complete phenotypic rescue remains elusive (Finkel et al., 2016; Chiriboga, 2017; McMillan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Existing SMA therapies primarily target postnatal treatment, potentially overlooking crucial developmental changes stemming from SMN depletion.
source: Additionally, existing therapies primarily target postnatal treatment, potentially overlooking crucial developmental changes stemming from SMN depletion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of current therapeutic interventions.

claim: Both clinical studies and preclinical mouse models have unveiled disruptions in fatty acid metabolism in SMA, leading to an increased susceptibility to dyslipidemia and liver steatosis.
source: Both clinical studies and preclinical mouse models have unveiled disruptions in fatty acid metabolism, leading to an increased susceptibility among SMA patients to dyslipidemia and liver steatosis (Deguise et al., 2019a; Crawford et al., 1999; Deguise et al., 2021a; Deguise et al., 2019b; Deguise et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The liver plays a multifaceted role in regulating numerous biological functions, including the storage and regulation of lipids, carbohydrates, amino acids, and iron, as well as the synthesis of essential growth factors and the clearance of toxic metabolites.
source: Given its multifaceted role in regulating numerous biological functions, including the storage and regulation of lipids, carbohydrates, amino acids, and iron, as well as the synthesis of essential growth factors and the clearance of toxic metabolites, any disruptions in liver function may have deleterious effects on other tissues (Trefts et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about liver function, supported by citation.

claim: Disruptions in liver function may have deleterious effects on other tissues.
source: Given its multifaceted role in regulating numerous biological functions, including the storage and regulation of lipids, carbohydrates, amino acids, and iron, as well as the synthesis of essential growth factors and the clearance of toxic metabolites, any disruptions in liver function may have deleterious effects on other tissues (Trefts et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the liver's central metabolic role, supported by citation.

claim: A transgenic mouse model featuring the Cre recombinase transgene driven by the α-fetoprotein promoter (Alfp-Cre) led to near-total depletion of SMN protein specifically in the liver, resulting in severe impairment of liver development and late embryonic lethality.
source: To explore the role of SMN in the liver, prior studies have utilized a transgenic mouse model featuring the Cre recombinase transgene driven by the α-fetoprotein promoter (Alfp-Cre). This approach led to near-total depletion of SMN protein specifically in the liver, resulting in severe impairment of liver development and late embryonic lethality (Vitte et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The Smn2B allele contains a 3-base pair substitution in the mouse Smn1 gene, resulting in aberrant splicing of exon 7.
source: The Smn2B allele contains a 3-base pair substitution in the mouse Smn1 gene, resulting in aberrant splicing of exon 7 (DiDonato et al., 2001; Hammond et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The genetic approach in the AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mouse model results in the production of approximately 30% full-length functional SMN protein production in the liver.
source: Consequently, this genetic approach results in the production of approximately 30% full-length functional SMN protein production in the liver.
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data showing ~70% reduction in SMN protein levels in the liver (Figure 1D and D').

claim: The AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mouse model induces mild liver steatosis at P19.
source: Our findings reveal that our novel liver-specific SMN depleted (herein referred to as AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7) mouse model induces mild liver steatosis and disrupts pancreatic function at postnatal day 19 (P19), characterized by decreased insulin-positive and increased glucagon-positive cells, alongside reduced blood glucose levels.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mouse model disrupts pancreatic function at P19, characterized by decreased insulin-positive and increased glucagon-positive cells.
source: Our findings reveal that our novel liver-specific SMN depleted (herein referred to as AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7) mouse model induces mild liver steatosis and disrupts pancreatic function at postnatal day 19 (P19), characterized by decreased insulin-positive and increased glucagon-positive cells, alongside reduced blood glucose levels.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both liver and pancreatic defects in the AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mouse model were rescued by P60.
source: However, both liver and pancreatic defects were rescued by P60.
evidence: This is supported by histological and functional data at P60 shown in Figure 7.

claim: The AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mouse model does not exhibit an overt SMA phenotype.
source: Remarkably, this mouse model does not exhibit an overt SMA phenotype, demonstrating normal lifespan and motor function.
evidence: This is supported by survival, weight, and motor function data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mouse model demonstrates normal lifespan.
source: Remarkably, this mouse model does not exhibit an overt SMA phenotype, demonstrating normal lifespan and motor function.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mouse model demonstrates normal motor function.
source: Remarkably, this mouse model does not exhibit an overt SMA phenotype, demonstrating normal lifespan and motor function.
evidence: This is supported by motor function tests shown in Figure 9E-G.

claim: There is an intricate relationship between hepatic function and pancreatic abnormalities in SMA.
source: Nevertheless, our data suggests an intricate relationship between hepatic function and pancreatic abnormalities in SMA, thereby enhancing our comprehension of the disease's pathophysiology.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that liver-specific SMN depletion affects pancreatic function.

claim: The Alb-Cre strain is commonly employed for liver-specific gene knockout using the Cre/loxP system.
source: To elucidate the impact of liver-specific SMN depletion on both CNS and peripheral tissue pathology, we utilized mice expressing Cre recombinase under the control of the mouse albumin promoter, referred to as AlbCre. This strain is commonly employed for liver-specific gene knockout using the Cre/loxP system (Postic et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Smn2B/- mice express approximately 15% residual full-length SMN compared to Smn2B/+ heterozygous mice.
source: Smn2B/- mice, the severe mouse model of SMA, express approximately 15% residual full-length SMN (FLSMN) compared to Smn2B/+ heterozygous mice (Eshraghi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: At P19, Smn2B/- mice show increased liver steatosis and metabolic defects.
source: At this stage, Smn2B/- mice show increased liver steatosis and metabolic defects, ultimately culminating in multiple system defects and mortality, typically occurring around P25 (Reilly et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Smn2B/- mice typically die around P25.
source: At this stage, Smn2B/- mice show increased liver steatosis and metabolic defects, ultimately culminating in multiple system defects and mortality, typically occurring around P25 (Reilly et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Smn2B/+ mice have slightly reduced levels of FLSMN and no overt phenotypical changes compared to wild-type mice.
source: In contrast, Smn2B/+ mice have slightly reduced levels of FLSMN and no overt phenotypical changes compared to wild-type mice (Bowerman et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: There was a ~70% decrease in FLSMN protein expression in the liver of AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice compared to littermate control counterparts (+/+;Smn2B/F7).
source: However, in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7, there was a~70% decrease in FLSMN protein expression in the liver (Figure 1D and D') compared to littermate control counterparts (+/+;Smn2B/F7).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1D and D'.

claim: SMN protein levels in the brain, muscle, spinal cord and pancreas remained unaltered in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice.
source: Conversely, SMN protein levels in the brain (Figure 1E and E'), muscle (Figure 1F and F'), spinal cord (Figure 1G and G') and pancreas (Figure 1H and H') remained unaltered, indicating that deletion of Smn exon 7 was restricted to the liver in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figures 1E-H.

claim: Deletion of Smn exon 7 was restricted to the liver in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice.
source: Conversely, SMN protein levels in the brain (Figure 1E and E'), muscle (Figure 1F and F'), spinal cord (Figure 1G and G') and pancreas (Figure 1H and H') remained unaltered, indicating that deletion of Smn exon 7 was restricted to the liver in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific SMN protein level data shown in Figures 1D-H.

claim: Cre expression was exclusively observed in the liver of AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice.
source: Cre expression was exclusively observed in the liver, where it exhibited variable expression across hepatocytes, with some cells showing detectable expression while others showed no expression, confirming the stochastic nature of Cre activity in our model.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cre activity in the AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 model is stochastic, with variable expression across hepatocytes.
source: Cre expression was exclusively observed in the liver, where it exhibited variable expression across hepatocytes, with some cells showing detectable expression while others showed no expression, confirming the stochastic nature of Cre activity in our model.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing mosaic Cre expression in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No Cre signal was detected in either the pancreas or spinal cord tissues of AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice.
source: No Cre signal was detected in either the pancreas or spinal cord tissues.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Smn2B/- mice exhibit defects in fatty acid metabolism and lipid accumulation in the liver.
source: We previously showed that Smn2B/- mice exhibit defects in fatty acid metabolism and lipid accumulation in the liver (Deguise et al., 2019a; Deguise et al., 2021a; Deguise et al., 2019b; Deguise et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research by the authors.

claim: SMA patients face an elevated risk of dyslipidemia and steatosis.
source: Additionally, SMA patients face an elevated risk of dyslipidemia and steatosis (Deguise et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Histology from AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice qualitatively indicates some level of hepatic microvesicular steatosis and lipid accumulation.
source: Histology from AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice (Figure 2A) qualitatively indicates some level of hepatic microvesicular steatosis and lipid accumulation.
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a noticeable variation in cell morphology and Oil Red-O retention among hepatocytes in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice, suggesting incomplete recombination.
source: However, there was a noticeable variation in cell morphology and Oil Red-O retention among hepatocytes, suggesting incomplete recombination.
evidence: This is inferred from the histological observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice showed variable triglycerides levels.
source: Consistent with the histological findings, AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice showed variable triglycerides levels (n1=45.95, n2=10.10; n3=75.72; n4=21.91 μg/mg, mean ± SEM 38.44±14.48) (Figure 2B), and yet higher than those observed in +/+;Smn2B/F7 controls (n1=2.60, n2=0.15; n3=0.66; n4=1.44 μg/mg, mean ± SEM 1.213±0.5332), although this difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.0824).
evidence: This is supported by triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Smn2B/- controls exhibited increased lipid accumulation and triglyceride levels.
source: As expected, Smn2B/- controls exhibited increased lipid accumulation and triglyceride levels.
evidence: This is supported by histological and biochemical data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The data suggest an intrinsic role of SMN in regulating fat liver metabolism.
source: Taken together, the data suggest an intrinsic role of SMN in regulating fat liver metabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of liver steatosis in liver-specific SMN-depleted mice.

claim: Smn2B/- mice show altered protein levels of heme oxygenase, transferrin, P62, and IGF-1 in the liver.
source: Specifically, we evaluated parameters associated with iron metabolism (Figure 2C, C', D and D'), endoplasmic reticulum stress (Figure 2E and E'), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; Figure 2F) levels, all of which have previously been identified as altered in Smn2B/- mice (Deguise et al., 2021b) and were further confirmed in our study.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and ELISA data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: No significant differences in the protein levels of heme oxygenase, transferrin, P62, and IGF-1 were found between the AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 and +/+;Smn2B/F7 control groups.
source: Our analysis revealed no significant differences in the protein levels of heme oxygenase, transferrin, P62, and IGF-1 between the AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 and +/+;Smn2B/F7 control groups.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and ELISA data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Liver-specific SMN depletion may not play a significant role in iron metabolism, endoplasmic reticulum stress, or IGF-1 pathways, or the mosaic nature of Cre-mediated excision led to a subtle effect that is difficult to detect.
source: These findings suggest that liver-specific SMN depletion may not play a significant role in these pathways or that the mosaic nature of Cre-mediated excision led to a subtle effect that is difficult to detect.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of significant changes in these markers despite liver steatosis.

claim: The Smn2B/- mouse model of SMA and type I SMA patients show pancreatic and glucose abnormalities.
source: We have demonstrated pancreatic and glucose abnormalities in the Smn2B/- mouse model of SMA and type I SMA patients (Bowerman et al., 2012b; Reilly et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research by the authors.

claim: AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice show a significant decrease in the proportion of β cells in the pancreas compared to +/+;Smn2B/F7 and Smn2B/+ heterozygous controls.
source: Surprisingly, double-labeling of insulin-producing β cells and glucagon-producing α cells revealed a significant decrease in the proportion of β cells and a notable increase in α cells in the pancreas of AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice compared to +/+;Smn2B/F7 and Smn2B/+ heterozygous controls (Figure 3A, B and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice show a notable increase in α cells in the pancreas compared to +/+;Smn2B/F7 and Smn2B/+ heterozygous controls.
source: Surprisingly, double-labeling of insulin-producing β cells and glucagon-producing α cells revealed a significant decrease in the proportion of β cells and a notable increase in α cells in the pancreas of AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice compared to +/+;Smn2B/F7 and Smn2B/+ heterozygous controls (Figure 3A, B and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A, F.

claim: AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice show reduced blood glucose levels relative to +/+;Smn2B/F7 and Smn2B/+.
source: Consequently, we evaluated non-fasting glucose levels in these mice (Figure 3C), revealing reduced blood glucose levels in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice relative to +/+;Smn2B/F7 and Smn2B/+.
evidence: This is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Blood glucose levels in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice remained higher than those observed in Smn2B/- mice.
source: However, blood glucose levels remained higher than those observed in Smn2B/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice show imbalances in α and β cell fate within pancreatic islets, resembling those observed in Smn2B/- mice.
source: Overall, these findings indicate imbalances in α and β cell fate within pancreatic islets in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice, resembling those observed in Smn2B/- mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Smn2B/- mice exhibit a normoinsulinemic plasma state, despite persistent hypoglycemia and reduced C-peptide levels at P19.
source: In previous work, we demonstrated that Smn2B/- mice exhibit a normoinsulinemic plasma state, despite persistent hypoglycemia and reduced C-peptide levels at P19 (Deguise et al., 2021a), findings that were recapitulated in this study (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice showed no significant changes in plasma insulin levels.
source: Similarly, AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice showed no significant changes in plasma insulin levels.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: C-peptide levels in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice were comparable to those observed in +/+;Smn2B/F7 and Smn2B/+ heterozygous controls.
source: However, surprisingly, C-peptide levels in these mice were comparable to those observed in +/+;Smn2B/F7 and Smn2B/+ heterozygous controls (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice show a marked increase in plasma glucagon levels.
source: Additionally, we observed a marked increase in plasma glucagon levels (Figure 3G) as well as elevated glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1) levels, a product of proglucagon processing (Figure 3H), reaching levels similar to those seen in Smn2B/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice show elevated glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1) levels.
source: Additionally, we observed a marked increase in plasma glucagon levels (Figure 3G) as well as elevated glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1) levels, a product of proglucagon processing (Figure 3H), reaching levels similar to those seen in Smn2B/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The increase in plasma glucagon and GLP-1 in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice likely reflects an increase in pancreatic α-cell numbers.
source: These changes likely reflect an increase in pancreatic α-cell numbers, although they were not accompanied by dysregulation of plasma pancreatic polypeptide (PP, Figure 3I) or amylin (Figure 3J) hormone production.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between increased α-cell numbers and elevated glucagon/GLP-1 levels.

claim: The changes in plasma glucagon and GLP-1 in AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 mice were not accompanied by dysregulation of plasma pancreatic polypeptide (PP) or amylin hormone production.
source: These changes likely reflect an increase in pancreatic α-cell numbers, although they were not accompanied by dysregulation of plasma pancreatic polypeptide (PP, Figure 3I) or amylin (Figure 3J) hormone production.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: The maintenance of SMN protein expression at levels comparable to those of heterozygous controls in the pancreas suggests that selective SMN depletion in the liver may be implicated in the dysfunction of the pancreas-liver axis.
source: Furthermore, the maintenance of SMN protein expression at levels comparable to those of heterozygous controls in the pancreas (Figure 1H and H') suggests that selective SMN depletion in the liver may be implicated in the dysfunction of the pancreas-liver axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pancreatic dysfunction occurs without changes in pancreatic SMN levels.

claim: The hallmark features of SMA include the degeneration of lower spinal motor neurons, neuromuscular junction (NMJ) pathology, and muscle atrophy.
source: The hallmark features of SMA include the degeneration of lower spinal motor neurons, neuromuscular junction (NMJ) pathology, and muscle atrophy (Bowerman et al., 2012a; Reilly et al., 2024; Deguise et al., 2016; Deguise et al., 2020; Gavrilina et al., 2008; Murray et al., 2013; Murray et al., 2015; Shababi et al., 2014; Lorson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SMA pathology, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Diminished levels of SMN protein are recognized as a pivotal factor in SMA pathology.
source: While the exact mechanisms linking these changes in the motor unit to the clinical manifestations of SMA remain unclear, diminished levels of SMN protein are recognized as a pivotal factor (Lefebvre et al., 1995; Lefebvre et al., 1997; Reilly et al., 2024; Lorson et al., 2010; Hua et al., 2011; Mercuri et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: No significant differences in motor neuron cell body counts were found among AlbCre/+;Smn2B/F7 and +/+;Smn2B/F7 and Smn2B/+ heterozygous controls.
